intro: Hindu texts have a long history, and they have traveled far. This unit follows that history, from the brick cities of the Indus valley to the Vedic age, from the time of the Upanishads and the Buddha to the Gupta kings and the great temples. You will see how scholars date each step, and how Hindu tradition tells the same story in its own terms.

Then you will follow the texts out of India. You will see them carved on the walls of Angkor Wat in Cambodia and acted out in shadow puppets in Bali. You will see American writers read the Gita at Walden Pond, and hear a monk speak in Chicago in 1893. You will also see how Gandhi, TV and Hindu American families have shaped them since.

By the end, you will be able to build a timeline that names scholarly and traditional dates side by side. You will explain hard topics, like the Manusmriti, with the range of responses. You will also trace how Hindu texts reached new readers, including in Illinois.
bigQuestion: How have Hindu texts changed and traveled through history, and how do we tell that history fairly?

timeline.t: The Indus cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro flourish
The Vedic period begins, by scholarly estimate
The age of the Upanishads, Mahavira and the Buddha
The Manusmriti and the Gita take shape, by scholarly estimate
The Gupta dynasty begins; temples and Puranas flourish
Suryavarman II begins Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu
Thoreau's Walden praises the Bhagavad Gita
Vivekananda speaks at the World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago
B.R. Ambedkar burns the Manusmriti in protest
U.S. immigration law changes; many Hindu families arrive
Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan airs on Indian TV

test.q: When did the Indus cities flourish?
test.why: The mature Indus civilization dates to about 2600–1900 BCE.

test.q: Why do scholars argue about the Pashupati seal?
test.why: With the script undeciphered, the seal's meaning is uncertain.

test.q: Who taught a middle way to end suffering?
test.why: The Buddha taught the middle way.
Ambedkar burned it to protest caste injustice.

test.q: Which temple in Cambodia shows the battle of Kurukshetra?
Where are most people Hindu in Indonesia?
test.why: Most people on Bali are Hindu.
Thoreau wrote Walden and admired the Gita.

test.q: What words began Vivekananda's 1893 Chicago address?
test.why: He began, 'Sisters and Brothers of America.'

test.q: How did Gandhi read the Gita's battle?
choices: As an allegory of inner struggle
test.why: Gandhi read it as an allegory.

test.q: When do many traditional counts begin the Kali Yuga?
test.why: Many traditional counts start it in 3102 BCE.

About what share of Americans are Hindu?
Which Gupta-age temple has carvings of Vishnu?
test.why: The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh dates to about 500 CE.

write.prompt: How has one Hindu text changed as it traveled? Pick the Gita or the Ramayana. Cite two or three moments from the unit, such as Gita 4.11 in Vivekananda's 1893 address, Gandhi's reading via Arnold's The Song Celestial (1885), or Angkor Wat's carvings, and explain how each reader or place used it.
tips: Name the text, verse or book, and the translation or source.
Give scholarly and traditional dates side by side when you date something.
Attribute every reading: "Gandhi read...", "many Hindus believe...".
Compare readers rather than judging them.
Use terms like diaspora, adaptation and allegory.
